claim: Project 'Setka': a nationwide UAP reporting network
evidence: A state programme ran 1978-1990 with a Defence Ministry topic and an Academy of Sciences topic; a General Staff directive of January 1980 told all military units to report sightings. Platov & Sokolov's English text calls the two topics 'DM Network' and 'AS Network'; Oleksiuk (2013) gives the Russian names 'Setka MO' and 'Setka AN' (setka = network). Correction to the earlier note that the name was absent: it is there, translated.

claim: The 'Blue Book' equivalent: Soviet military UAP files
evidence: The Defence Ministry branch existed (main executor a central military research institute near Moscow). No released military case file was found on archive.org, CREST or the hosts reachable from here; the programme's own summary is the best open source.

claim: Soviet scientists published on UAP in Priroda and Zemlya i Vselennaya
evidence: archive.org holds 2 Zemlya i Vselennaya issues (1972-05, 1978 No.4) with 0 UFO keyword hits and no Soviet-era Priroda issues; priroda.ras.ru, cyberleninka.ru and elibrary.ru are unreachable from this container; Priroda 2015 No.8 has no UFO article; the academic-journal piece found (Oleksiuk 2013) cites only Vestnik RAN 2000. The Soviet academic output that is verified is the Gindilis et al. 1979 preprint (NASA TM-75665).

claim: Soviet pilots, radar operators and cosmonauts reported UAP
evidence: The native chronicle has aircrew, radar and missile-range entries (counts in the report), all as retellings without primary documents; no cosmonaut testimony was found in it. The 1948-49 Apraksin chases have no documentary trace here.

claim: AAWSAP DIRDs reference Soviet 'Thread-3' technology assessments
evidence: 0 hits for 'Thread-3'/'Thread 3' in 37 DIRDs, 286 PURSUE server files and the PURSUE OCR; DIRD mentions of the Soviet Union are unrelated to UAP.

claim: The PLA has its own UAP research program
evidence: Open sources show a civilian association, CURO (set up 1978, member of the China Association for Science and Technology), and a 1980 Wuhan University survey. Nothing in CREST/JPRS or Xinhua texts on disk describes a PLA programme.

claim: China is the only other superpower with a systematic UAP research program
evidence: See C06; the Chinese effort found is civilian and amateur-academic.

claim: Arabic-language UAP reports are completely absent from the English-language corpus
evidence: Hatch has 148 Arab-world entries (Algeria 54, Morocco 44, Tunisia 10, other 40). The most-reprinted Egyptian book is a compilation of Western cases (America 38-39 mentions, Egypt 0) with no native case.

claim: The deep term search found extensive discussion of vimana in the DIRD literature
evidence: 0 hits for vimana/Sanskrit/Mahabharata in DIRDs and PURSUE; one 'Ramayana' mention in the COMETA report file.

claim: Sanskrit epics describe aerial vehicles that parallel modern UAP descriptions
evidence: The epics use vimana (e.g. Pushpaka) with no flight mechanism. The only 'technical' vimana text, the Vymanika Shastra, was composed 1900-1922 (IISc 1974: 'cannot be dated earlier than 1904') and none of its craft could fly.

claim: Simultaneous sightings: the same event in Russian and US databases
evidence: Russian native vs NUFORC same-day rate ratio 1.01; vs GEIPAN 1.07 (date-shift null); positive control Hatch US vs NUFORC same day within 100 km gives 5.6.

claim: Unique Soviet reports exist (events only in the Russian corpus)
evidence: Over 90% of each catalogue's Soviet events have no counterpart in the other (date +-1 day, <=800 km).

claim: Soviet and American observers use different descriptive frameworks
evidence: Disc is 26% of first shapes in English Hatch SU entries vs 9% in the Russian chronicle (p=0.0002); plume words are Soviet-specific. But Hatch US vs NUFORC differ by TVD 0.25, so compiler effects are as large as language effects.

claim: Soviet UAP cluster near Soviet nuclear facilities
evidence: Russian chronicle: 0 within 30 km vs 2.2 expected; its 100 km excess is Moscow-Obninsk / St Petersburg-Leningrad NPP and turns into a deficit without Moscow. Hatch SU: reactors 4 vs 1.1 at 30 km (two of the four are reports about the plant itself); 50 km excess is the Voronezh 1989 wave. The site list misses most closed weapons cities.

claim: Platov & Sokolov: over 90% of anomalous phenomena were rocket effects plus balloons
evidence: Plume-worded Russian reports fall on Soviet launch days (UTC) more than date-shifted copies do (RR 1.47, p=0.029; within 1,500 km of Plesetsk RR 1.80, p=0.026); non-plume reports do not (RR 1.08). Window W0 was not pre-registered, so this is suggestive.
NASA TM-75665 (translation of Pr-473, 1979) and TM-75761 records found; full text not reached.
